'''''Protea neriifolia''''', also known as the '''narrow-leaf sugarbush''',<ref name=SANBI>{{cite web |last1=Rebelo |first1=A.G. |last2=Mtshali |first2=H. |last3=von Staden |first3=L. |title=Narrow-leaved Sugarbush |website=Red List of South African Plants |version=version 2020.1 |date=10 June 2019 |publisher=[[South African National Biodiversity Institute]] |url=http://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=799-94 |access-date=20 July 2020}}</ref><ref name=BioEx>{{cite web |title=''Protea neriifolia'' (Narrow-leaf sugarbush) |url=http://biodiversityexplorer.info/plants/proteaceae/protea_neriifolia.htm |website=Biodiversity Explorer |publisher=Iziko - Museums of South Africa |access-date=21 July 2020}}</ref><ref name=ProAtlWeb>{{Cite web |url=https://www.proteaatlas.org.za/sugar2.htm |title=Bearded Sugarbushes - ''Proteas'' |date=11 March 1998 |website=Protea Atlas Project Website |access-date=20 July 2020}}</ref> '''oleander-leaved sugarbush''',<ref name=SANBI/>  '''blue sugarbush''',<ref name=SANBI/><ref name=vanWyk1997>{{cite book |last=van Wyk |first=Braam |last2=van Wyk |first2=Piet |date=1997 |title=Field Guide to trees of South Africa |location=Cape Town |publisher=Struik |pages=216, 217 |isbn=1-86825-922-6}}</ref> or the '''oleanderleaf protea''',{{citation needed|date=July 2020}} is a [[flowering plant]] in the genus ''[[Protea]]'',<ref name=ProAtlWeb/> which is [[endemism|endemic]] to [[South Africa]].<ref name=SANBI/>

[[Common name]]s for the species in the [[Afrikaans language]] include ''blousuikerbos'',<ref name=vanWyk1997/> ''baardsuikerbos'',<ref name=SANBI/> ''baardsuikerkan'',<ref name=SANBI/> ''blou-suikerbos'',<ref name=SANBI/> ''blousuikerkan'',<ref name=SANBI/> ''roosboom''<ref name=SANBI/> and ''suikerbos''.<ref name=SANBI/>

The tree's national number is 93.1.<ref name=vanWyk1997/><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.treetags.co.za/national-list-of-indigenous-trees/|title=National List of Indigenous Trees}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
Although it was first discovered by Europeans in 1597, and was the subject of a botanical illustration in 1605,{{citation needed|date=July 2020}} the plant was first [[Species description|described]] as a distinct species according to the modern Linnaean system by the naturalist [[Robert Brown (botanist, born 1773)|Robert Brown]] in his 1810 treatise ''[[On the Proteaceae of Jussieu]]''.<ref name=IPNI/>

==Description==
It is a large, erect [[shrub]] or small tree,<ref name=ProAtlWeb/><ref name=vanWyk1997/> growing from about three<ref name=ProAtlWeb/><ref name=Weaver1982>Weaver, C. (producer) 1982. pp. 50–56 ''Wildlife Through the Camera''. 1982. British Broadcasting Corporation {{ISBN|0-563-20069-3}}</ref> to five metres in height.<ref name=Weaver1982/> The stems become [[Glabrousness (botany)|glabrous]] (hairless) when mature.<ref name=vanWyk1997/>

The leaves are 'sessile', which means they lack a petiole and arise straight from the stems. These leaves diagnostically curve upwards. They are elliptic-shaped, coloured green or blue-grey, and their margin run parallel to each other. The leaves become glabrous when mature.<ref name=vanWyk1997/>

It blooms in Summer and Spring,<ref name=vanWyk1997/> although it has also been seen blooming in the Winter and Autumn.<ref name=BioEx/> The plant is [[monoecious]], with both sexes in each flower.<ref name=ProAtlWeb/> It has its flowers arranged in a [[head (botany)|flower head]], a special type of [[inflorescence]].{{citation needed|date=July 2020}} Each branch bears only one inflorescence. This species is recognisable in having the inflorescence shaped as a long, oblong cone. It is 13 by 8 cm in size.<ref name=vanWyk1997/> The flower heads are cup-shaped, and the flowers within them contain [[nectar]].<ref name=Weaver1982/> The inflorescence is subtended (i.e. surrounded or covered) by 'involucral [[bract]]s'.<ref name=vanWyk1997/> These outer bracts range in colour from carmine to pink to creamy-green or whitish, this colour contrasts with the characteristic hairy black fringe on the margins of the apex of the bract.<ref name=BioEx/><ref name=vanWyk1997/><ref name=Weaver1982/> The inner bracts are shaped oblong to spatulate, and are typically curved inwards at the tips. These tips are rounded and also covered in a black, sometimes white, beard of fuzzy hairs.<ref name=vanWyk1997/>

The fruit is a [[Nut (fruit)|nut]], its surface densely covered in hairs.<ref name=vanWyk1997/> These small nuts are packed together within the dried inflorescence, which remains on the plant after [[Plant senescence|senescence]]. When eventually released, the seeds are dispersed by means of the wind.<ref name=ProAtlWeb/>

===Similar species===
It is similar to ''[[Protea laurifolia]]'', whose flower heads also possess a hairy black fringe on their bracts, a species found further to the west. ''P. laurifolia'' can be distinguished by means of its leaves having a very short petiole, these leaves have a heavy horny margin and are usually more bluish or silvery-coloured than those of ''P. neriifolia''.<ref name=vanWyk1997/>

==Distribution==
''Protea neriifolia'' occurs in both the [[Western Cape|Western]] and the [[Eastern Cape]] provinces of [[South Africa]].<ref name=SANBI/> It occurs in the southern coastal mountain ranges of [[South Africa]], between [[Cape Town]] and [[Port Elizabeth]].{{citation needed|date=July 2020}} It grows in the mountain ranges of [[Hottentots Holland Mountains|Hottentots Holland]], [[Langeberg]], [[Groot Winterhoek]], [[Elandsberg]], [[Rooiberg Mountains|Rooiberg]], [[Kammanassie Mountains|Kammanassie]], [[Potberg]],<ref name=ProAtlWeb/> [[Riviersonderend]],<ref name=BioEx/><ref name=ProAtlWeb/> [[Kogelberg]] and [[Jonkershoek Nature Reserve|Jonkershoek]], as well as at [[Garcia's Pass]]<ref name=BioEx/> and near the towns of [[Tulbagh]] and [[Ceres, Western Cape|Ceres]].<ref name=ProAtlWeb/>

==Ecology==
The species is encountered in [[fynbos]] amongst [[restio]]s. It usually is found growing in dense stands on south-facing slopes,<ref name=BioEx/><ref name=vanWyk1997/> sometimes occurring together with ''[[Leucadendron xanthoconus]]''.<ref name=BioEx/> It grows on sandy,<ref name=vanWyk1997/> and in [[sandstone]]-, or occasionally [[granite]], derived soils. It is found at altitudes ranging from [[sea level]] to {{Convert|1300|m}}. During the [[wildfire]]s which periodically occur in this type of [[habitat]], mature plants of this species are destroyed, but the seeds are able to survive such events.<ref name=ProAtlWeb/>

The flowers are [[Pollination|pollinated]] by birds,<ref name=ProAtlWeb/> which are attracted by the insects and nectar, as well as various insects including [[Trichostetha fascicularis|protea beetles]] and [[Scarabaeidae|scarab beetles]].{{citation needed|date=July 2020}}

Plants at the [[Kirstenbosch Botanic Gardens]] have their flowers visited by the Cape sugarbird (''[[Promerops cafer]]'').<ref name=BioEx/>

==Horticulture ==
''Protea neriifolia'' is highly adaptable to cultivation under garden conditions, and is among the most widely grown of the protea species. It is also extensively grown commercially for [[cut flowers]], not only in its native South Africa,<ref name=vanWyk1997/> but also in Australia, New Zealand, the United States and other countries with climatically suitable areas. In addition to selected cultivars, such as 'Green Ice', 'Margaret Watling' and 'Silvertips', the species has been crossed to produce several hybrids, such as 'Carnival' ([[Protea compacta|''P. compacta'']] x ''P. neriifolia''),{{citation needed|date=July 2020}} or perhaps 'Pink Mink'.<ref name=smgrow>{{cite web |url=https://www.smgrowers.com/products/plants/plantdisplay.asp?plant_id=2352 |title=''Protea laurifolia'' 'Rose Mink' |author=<!--Not stated--> |website=www.smgrowers.com |publisher=San Marcos Growers |access-date=20 July 2020}}</ref>

==Conservation==
This species is not threatened.<ref name=ProAtlWeb/> The population numbers are believed to be stable. The [[South African National Biodiversity Institute]] assessed the conservation status of the species as '[[least concern]]' in 2009, and again in 2019.<ref name=SANBI/>
